topics.summary: HarborWorks can package the status site’s runtime in a container, but the host remains responsible for security, storage, networking, and supervision. A container is not a miniature universe in which administrative consequences disappear. This chapter treats it as an ordinary process with explicit isolation and packaging mechanisms.

topics.summary: A conventional Linux container shares the host kernel while using isolation mechanisms to provide separate views and controls. A VM runs a guest kernel against virtual hardware. blocks.text: A conventional Linux container shares the host kernel while using isolation mechanisms to provide separate views and controls. A VM runs a guest kernel against virtual hardware. Containers often start quickly and package applications compactly, but kernel compatibility and the host trust boundary remain important.

Choose from workload requirements. A need for a different guest kernel or stronger separation can favor a VM or another isolation technology. A reproducible userspace application with controlled host integration may fit a container well.

Neither choice provides high availability by itself. A container restarted on one failed disk cannot recover data that existed only on that disk. Packaging, orchestration, persistence, and disaster recovery are separate decisions.

topics.title: 26.2 Namespaces
topics.summary: Namespaces give processes different views of selected system resources, such as process IDs, mounts, networking, and user identities. A process can see PID 1 inside its namespace while having another PID from the host’s perspective.

blocks.text: Namespaces give processes different views of selected system resources, such as process IDs, mounts, networking, and user identities. A process can see PID 1 inside its namespace while having another PID from the host’s perspective.

Isolation is selective. Sharing the host network namespace removes a network boundary; bind-mounting host directories exposes those paths. User namespaces can map identities differently between container and host. “Root inside” is not a complete statement without those mappings and privileges.

Diagnose from the relevant view. A listener visible inside a container may not be published on the host. A file path inside the image may be hidden by a runtime volume mount. Inspect the actual runtime configuration rather than the Containerfile alone.
Linux example — 26.2
Read namespace identities of the current shell.
ls -l /proc/$$/ns

topics.title: 26.3 Control Groups
topics.summary: Control groups account for and control groups of processes. Container runtimes use them to implement resource policies where the host and permissions support those controls. A CPU quota limits time allocation; a memory ceiling can trigger a container-scoped failure before the host is globally full.

blocks.text: Control groups account for and control groups of processes. Container runtimes use them to implement resource policies where the host and permissions support those controls. A CPU quota limits time allocation; a memory ceiling can trigger a container-scoped failure before the host is globally full.

Set limits from tests, not aesthetics. Too-small memory limits can make an otherwise correct application repeatedly fail; no limits can allow one workload to harm its neighbors. Observe throttling, pressure, and termination events alongside application behavior.

On rootless systems, available control depends on cgroup version and delegation. A command accepting a resource option is not sufficient evidence that the intended policy is enforced. Inspect the effective runtime and measure behavior in a lab. (R16)
Linux example — 26.3
Inspect container resource usage without an endless display.
podman stats --no-stream

blocks.text: An image describes filesystem layers and runtime defaults. A running container adds writable state and selected mounts. Replacing the container does not necessarily preserve changes made only in its writable layer.

Tags are names that can move to different image content. A digest identifies particular content, subject to platform-manifest details. For reproducible deployment, record the resolved digest, architecture, build inputs, and configuration. A digest proves content identity, not that the image is trustworthy or free of vulnerabilities.

Keep secrets out of build layers. Deleting a secret in a later layer does not reliably remove it from earlier published layers. Use approved build-time secret facilities and runtime secret delivery instead of copying credentials into an image.

podman images --digests

blocks.text: A registry distributes images and associated metadata. Use fully qualified references to avoid ambiguous short-name resolution. Authenticate through approved tooling, verify transport trust, and protect registry credentials.

Decide what happens when the registry is unavailable during recovery. Pre-pulling a reviewed image or maintaining an approved internal mirror can reduce a dependency, but cached content still needs lifecycle management and security review.

Distinguish scanning, signatures, and provenance. A scan reports selected known issues under its current database. Signature verification checks an identity or policy attached to an artifact. Provenance describes its build history under a trust model. None replaces testing the application and its privileges.

blocks.text: Docker commonly uses a client communicating with an engine that manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. Access to a powerful daemon socket can permit operations with host-level consequences. Do not treat membership in a Docker administration group as a harmless convenience for untrusted users.

A Dockerfile describes build steps, while the run configuration determines mounts, ports, identities, capabilities, and resource limits. A secure-looking Dockerfile can be undermined by --privileged or by mounting the host root filesystem at runtime.

Rootless operation is a separate supported arrangement with its own prerequisites and limitations. Review the installed engine’s security documentation rather than assuming every Docker installation has identical privilege boundaries. (R57)

blocks.text: Volumes and bind mounts provide runtime data outside the container’s disposable writable layer. A named volume is managed by the runtime; a bind mount exposes a specified host path. Both require backup ownership and an access policy.

A read-only bind mount can protect release content from container writes. On SELinux hosts, relabel options such as :Z and :z have distinct private-versus-shared intent and can change labels on host content. Never apply them casually to broad system directories or a home directory containing unrelated data.

User-namespace mapping also affects ownership. Do not recursively change host ownership to a guessed container UID. Inspect the mapping and use the runtime’s supported tools on a dedicated data tree. (R56)

blocks.text: Reduce the image to needed software, run with an appropriate non-root identity, remove unnecessary capabilities, avoid privileged mode, limit mounts, and restrict network paths. Retain host SELinux or AppArmor and the runtime’s applicable syscall filtering.

The container runtime socket is a sensitive control interface, not a routine application volume. Mounting it into a web application can expose the host’s orchestration powers. Similarly, a read-only image does not protect data on a separately writable host mount.

Patch both image and host. Rebuilding an image is not deployment, and deployment is not verification that all old instances are gone. Track the exact running artifact and test that rollback remains compatible with retained data.

labs.title: Preserve data outside an ephemeral runtime directory
labs.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT
cd -- "$lab_dir"
mkdir runtime durable
printf 'saved\n' > durable/state
printf 'ephemeral\n' > runtime/cache
rm runtime/cache
rmdir runtime
test "$(cat durable/state)" = saved
printf 'runtime removed; durable fixture retained\n'
